title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (E420, 1771-72). Euler varies the integral J = ∫Z dx, with dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + ... and p = dy/dx, q = dp/dx. The variation is generated by an auxiliary parameter t: δy = dt (dy/dt). After integration by parts the variation has two parts. The first is ∫δy (N − P' + Q'' − ...) dx; it vanishes for all admissible variations iff the Euler–Lagrange equation holds (§38, previous page). The second is the boundary term [δy (P − dQ/dx + ddR/dx² − ...)] evaluated at the end M minus its value at the start A.

On this page:
§39: At M, dt(dy/dt) is the vertical segment Mμ; at A it is Aα. So if every neighbouring curve αμ passes through both A and M (fixed endpoints), the boundary part vanishes.
§40: Now let the neighbouring curve pass through A but end at μ, vertically displaced from M. The boundary variation is Mμ·H, with H = P − Q' + R'' − ... Next let the curve end at an arbitrary infinitely near point ω, with abscissa increment Pp = dx. One must add the extra piece of the integral over that increment, Z·Pp. The variation is then Mμ·H + Z·Pp.
§41 (begun here, finished on p.60): draw Mω and let ω be the angle ωMm with the principal curve. Since mω ≈ Mμ and the tangent of angle mMo is p, we have Oω = Mμ + p·Pp. Then tan ω = Mμ/(Pp(1+p²) + p·Mμ), so Mμ = Pp(1+p²)tan ω/(1 − p tan ω). The variation becomes Pp[Z + (1+p²)tan ω/(1 − p tan ω)·H].

In modern terms: with δx = Pp and δy = Mμ + p δx, the variation is H(δy − p δx) + Z δx = (Z − pH)δx + H δy. This is the general variable-endpoint formula. Requiring it to vanish for endpoints on a given line gives the transversality condition Z + H(s − p) = 0, where s is the slope of the line. For the line normal to the curve (s = −1/p) this gives pZ = (1+p²)H. When Z depends only on x, y, p, this means Z = g(x,y)√(1+p²). That is exactly the class of integrands for which transversality reduces to orthogonality.
errors: The boundary term keeps only the δy-coefficient P − Q' + R'' − ... When Z contains q, r, ..., the full boundary term also contains δp·(Q − R' + ...) + δq·(R − ...) + ... Euler's free-endpoint formula is therefore complete only when Z depends on x, y, p alone (or when δp, δq, ... vanish at the ends).
Everything is first order ('proxime'): Z·Pp, mω ≈ Mμ, and the angle formula all neglect second-order terms. This is consistent with a first-variation computation.

ideas.what: Vanishing of boundary terms for fixed endpoints
ideas.modern_name: Fixed-endpoint boundary terms in the first variation
ideas.where_published: E296 Elementa calculi variationum (1766), E297; E420

ideas.what: Variation for an endpoint moved vertically: Mμ·(P − Q' + R'' ...)
ideas.where_published: E296/E297, Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385)

ideas.what: General moving-endpoint variation Z δx + H(δy − p δx), and the angle making it vanish
ideas.where_published: E420 itself; similar endpoint discussion in Lagrange's Essai (Misc. Taur. 1760-61); Euler's Methodus inveniendi (1744) treated some variable-endpoint cases

ideas.what: Condition pZ = (1+p²)H for the transversal to be normal to the extremal (continued on p.60)
ideas.modern_name: Orthogonality of transversality; integrands of the form g(x,y)√(1+p²) (conformal/Riemannian length)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Kneser / Darboux era (orthogonal trajectories of geodesic fields; Gauss's lemma for geodesics)
ideas.where_published: E420 §42 (next page); not sure Euler integrates it further

missed.claim: Euler's question 'for which Z is the transversal normal to the extremal?' leads, for Z = Z(x,y,p), to the characterization Z = g(x,y)√(1+p²). This is the classical fact that transversality equals orthogonality exactly for (conformally) Riemannian length functionals, a theme of Kneser and of Gauss's geodesic-polar lemma. Euler poses it as a condition on the 'indoles' of Z. The posing itself is somewhat early, though the content is well known.
missed.quote: Ducatur recta Mω et quaeramus angulum ωMm, quem haec recta Mω cum curua principali constituit
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of historical interest: an early instance of transversality as a geometric angle condition. The modern theory is complete.

deep.surprise_reason: The page carries the standard boundary/natural-endpoint terms and sets up a transversality computation that is well known and published (in this very paper). The only mildly notable feature is the geometric angle formulation leading to the normal-transversal condition, which is completed on the next page.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially accurate. In 'ideoque om' the word 'om' is the catchword continuing on p.60 ('om = p.Pp'). 'Pp = dx' is the abscissa increment at the end, written Pp in the original.
